title: What To Do If the Police Stop or Arrest You
summary: Your rights during a police stop, questioning or arrest, and the small steps that protect you.
sectionRefs: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)

body.text: Being stopped or arrested by the police is frightening. Knowing a few clear rules keeps the situation calm and protects you. These rules come from the Constitution and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which replaced the old CrPC.
If you are only stopped or questioned

items: Stay calm and polite. Do not argue or run.
You may ask the officer for their name and police station.
You are not required to answer questions that could incriminate you.
For a vehicle check, you must show your licence and documents.
You have the right to know the reason for your arrest (Article 22(1)).
You have the right to inform a family member or friend.
You must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (Article 22(2)).
You have the right to a lawyer of your choice, and to free legal aid if you cannot afford one.
You cannot be forced to confess. Statements made under threat are not valid (Article 20(3)).

body.text: A woman cannot normally be arrested after sunset and before sunrise, except in exceptional cases with a magistrate's permission and a woman officer present.
You are entitled to a medical examination and to have your arrest recorded in a memo signed by a witness.
For a bailable offence, you have the right to be released on bail. The police should tell you this.

practicalSteps: Note the time, place and the officers' names or badge numbers.
Tell one trusted person where you are and who took you.
Ask for the grounds of arrest in writing.
Do not sign any blank or unread paper.
Ask for a lawyer, or call the NALSA helpline 15100 for free legal aid.
exceptions: Preventive detention laws allow detention without a normal charge, but with safeguards and periodic review.
In some serious offences an arrest may be made without a warrant, but the 24-hour rule still applies.

faqs.q: Can the police search my phone or home without a warrant?
faqs.a: A search generally needs a warrant or a clear legal basis, except in specific situations such as with your consent, during a lawful arrest, or under a specific legal provision. Ask for the legal basis.

faqs.q: What if the police refuse to register my complaint?
faqs.a: You can send your complaint to the Superintendent of Police, file a complaint before the Magistrate under the BNSS, or use your state police online complaint portal.

sources.label: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 - India Code

misconceptions.myth: The police can keep me as long as they want before a court hearing.
misconceptions.fact: No. Article 22(2) requires you to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours of arrest.
